Công ty trách nhiệm hữu hạn cổ phần sáu thành viên lục long hội

Phát huy sức mạnh đoàn kết toàn dân tộc

Hiện đại hóa đất nước Việt Nam 

Chung tay góp sức vì một tương lai tươi đẹp
summary:
Every dry season, rice farmers on the coast of Sóc Trăng make the same bet. Plant a third crop and hope the salt water stays out of the canals, or leave the field empty and lose the income. This year NOAA is forecasting a strong El Niño, and that bet is about to get much harder.

We built Mekong Rotation Explorer to help with that choice. It’s a free website, in Vietnamese and English, made for the phone a farmer already has. They tap their area on a map and tell us what matters most to them: saving water, making money, keeping the soil healthy, or staying safe from salt. The site then compares five realistic ways to rotate their crops, including what they grow now, and explains each one in plain words: why it might work, what could go wrong, and how sure we really are.

It also works as a dashboard. Farmers can keep all their fields in one place, see what’s coming each month, and follow a 12-month plan they can print, share or listen to.

Everything is built on NASA rainfall, weather and satellite data. It doesn’t replace the farmer’s own judgement. It just helps them plan before the salt arrives.
details:
What it does

Think of it as a planning companion with a dashboard attached.

When you open the site, the first thing you see is the coast right now: what month it is, roughly how many weeks until the salt usually shows up, and a short checklist of things to do before it does. From there you pick your area on a satellite map. We cover five places, from Vĩnh Châu right on the coast to Ngã Năm further inland. A slider lets you scroll through the months and watch which areas the salt reaches, and when.

Next, you tell the site about yourself: what you grow now, what you care about most (four simple sliders), and whether brackish water is an option for you. It then lays out five rotations side by side: triple rice, double rice, rice with shrimp, rice with an upland crop like watermelon, maize or mung bean, and salt-tolerant rice. Each one gets a card with scores, a crop calendar, the reasons behind it, the risks, and links to every source. Each card also says how confident we are, because some options rest on far better evidence than others.

Pick one and you get a full 12-month plan: when to sow, what seed and fertiliser you’ll need, and what to watch for. You can print it, send it to someone, or have it read aloud in Vietnamese, which matters to farmers who don’t read easily.

The dashboard

Most farmers have more than one field, and each field behaves differently. In “My fields” you can save each one with its own plan and size, and see a rough cost and income estimate for it. You can also flip between a normal year, an El Niño year and the last 12 months, and see how the picture changes. If you have an idea of your own, the Plan Lab lets you test it against the same data. Everything is saved on your own phone, so there’s no account and no sign-up.

How it works

Behind the scenes, a small Python pipeline pulls in the data and boils it down into one file the website reads:

  • NASA GPM rainfall going back to 2000.
  • NASA POWER daily weather, which we use to work out how thirsty each crop is and how many days get too hot.
  • NASA MODIS satellite greenness, which shows how many crops a field really grows each year and when it lies bare.
  • NASA Black Marble night imagery for the map.
  • SoilGrids soil data and NOAA El Niño forecasts.
  • Published salinity records from eight river and canal stations, covering 25 years.

We kept the scoring simple and open. Every formula is written out in our README. We chose not to use machine learning, because there isn’t enough real outcome data to train a model honestly, and a confident-sounding guess is the last thing a farmer needs.

Being straight with people

No satellite can measure salt in water, so every salinity number on the site is clearly marked as an estimate from public reports. When a score depends on a guess our team had to make, its confidence drops a level and the card says so. As a sanity check, we looked at whether the NASA data picks out droughts people already remember. It does: four of the five driest seasons it finds were El Niño years.

What we used

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map, hosted for free on GitHub Pages. The pipeline is Python with only the standard library, so anyone can rerun it without installing anything.

What we thought about

We kept coming back to one person: a farmer with a phone, maybe a slow connection, maybe not much time to read, who knows their land far better than we do. That’s why the site works in two languages and reads plans aloud. It’s also why it shows its sources instead of asking for trust, and why every plan ends with a nudge to talk it over with the local extension officer. The same approach can be reused for other parts of the Delta, and the README explains how.

MODIS Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 250m (MOD13Q1 v6.1)
NASA AppEEARS (Application for Extracting and Exploring Analysis Ready Samples)
NASA GIBS – VIIRS Black Marble Night Lights
Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 Vegetation Indices, Landsat (HLSL30 VI v2.0)
